L7.66: Algorithm for the management of elevated low density lipoprotein cholesterol in adults without cardiovascular disease. Is LDL-C >= 190 mg/dL? Yes: Evaluate patient for FH. FH present: Follow treatment recommendations for FH. FH absent: Start high-intensity statin therapy. No: Calculate 10-year cardiovascular disease risk. >10%: Start moderate-dose statin, repeat LDL-C in 6 weeks, has LDL-C fallen by expected amount (30 to 50%)? Yes: Continue moderate-dose statin or consider high-intensity statin if 10-year risk >= 20% and LDL-C > 100 mg/dL. No: Evaluate patient compliance. 5 to 10%: Discuss statin with patient (shared decision making). In some patients, consider additional risk stratification such as with a calcium score or lipoprotein(a) level. <5%: Follow recommendations for repeat screening. This algorithm applies to all adult men and women between the ages of 18 and 75 years. FH: familial hypercholesterolemia.

L6.108: All motivated hypertensive patients should receive counseling about lifestyle interventions to lower BP. Is the systolic pressure >20 mmHg above the goal and/or the diastolic pressure >10 mmHg above the goal? Yes: Initiate an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) plus a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. No: ACR >= 300 mg/g? Yes: Initiate an ACE inhibitor (or ARB). No: Initiate an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) or a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. BP remains uncontrolled: Combine an ACE inhibitor (or ARB) and a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. BP remains uncontrolled: Add a thiazide-like diuretic. BP remains uncontrolled: Apparent resistant hypertension. Inset 1 Reasons to incorporate other agents earlier in the treatment regimen include: A thiazide-like diuretic is useful in patients with osteoporosis, edema, calcium nephrolithiasis with hypercalciuria. A beta blocker should generally be used initially in patients with a history of myocardial infarction. A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is appropriate in patients with HFpEF. Drugs such as ARNIs, beta blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists should be used initially in patients with HFrEF. Inset 2 BP control should be reassessed approximately 4 weeks after initiation or titration of therapy. 1 or 2 titration steps are appropriate before modifying or adding medication (because titrating drugs to their maximum dose increases the risk of adverse effects while providing diminishing benefits on BP control). The most common causes of lack of response to antihypertensive drug therapy are: 1. Medication nonadherence 2. White coat effect 3. Improper BP measurement. Thus, when drug therapy interventions appear to be ineffective, the clinician should consider nonadherence and ensure that BP is evaluated properly.

L8.26: Mechanism figure. Nitrates (nitric oxide) stimulate conversion of GTP to cGMP, which activates protein kinase G and lowers cytosolic calcium, causing smooth muscle relaxation, vasodilation and lower blood pressure. PDE5 breaks cGMP down to inactive GMP. Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil inhibit PDE5. Figure: drug interaction between type 5 PDE inhibitors and nitrates.

L8.34: Antianginals and comorbid conditions. Co-morbidity, first line therapy, alternatives, avoid. Hypertension: first line beta blocker, alternative non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (NDHP). Prior myocardial infarction: first line beta blocker, avoid calcium channel blockers. Decreased left ventricular function: first line beta blocker, alternative amlodipine, avoid other calcium channel blockers. Bradycardia or atrioventricular block: first line dihydropyridine (DHP), alternative long-acting nitrate, avoid non-dihydropyridines and beta blockers. Diabetes: first line non-dihydropyridine, alternatives long-acting nitrate and cardioselective beta blocker, avoid non-cardioselective beta blocker. Asthma: first line non-dihydropyridine and cardioselective beta blocker, avoid non-cardioselective beta blocker.
L8.41: Acute coronary syndrome classification figure. Ischemic discomfort leads to a working diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome. ECG with no ST elevation: unstable angina or non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI, also called non-Q-wave myocardial infarction). ECG with ST elevation: Q-wave myocardial infarction. A biochemical marker separates unstable angina from myocardial infarction. Below it, heart cross-sections at 1 hour, 4 hours and 8 hours show the infarct (dark) growing into the area of ischemia (light).
L8.42: Thrombus formation. Blood vessel with atherosclerotic plaque: endothelium, smooth muscle cells, fibrous cap and plaque.
L8.43: Thrombus formation. Procedural injury, for example balloon deployment, or spontaneous injury both leave injured endothelium.
L8.44: Thrombus formation. Platelet adhesion, activation and aggregation at the plaque.
L8.47: Thrombus formation. Thrombin is the link between tissue injury, coagulation and platelet response. Collagen releases adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and thromboxane A2, which activate and aggregate platelets. Tissue factor starts the plasma clotting cascade, prothrombin becomes thrombin, and thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin, forming the thrombus. Thrombin is a critical mediator in coagulation and elicits multiple responses in platelets.
L8.48: Thrombus formation, initiation. Tissue factor complexes with factor VIIa formed at the site of tissue injury, activates factor X and factor IX, and generates small amounts of thrombin.
L8.49: Thrombus formation, amplification. Thrombin activates platelets, stimulates its own production by activating factors V and VIII, also activates factor XI, and coagulation factors (VIIIa, Va, IXa) assemble on the surface of activated platelets.
L8.50: Thrombus formation, propagation. Assembled complexes continue the cascade on the surface of activated platelets: conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, and clot stabilization.
